intro: Judith Bokor plays “Le Cygne”, the thirteenth movement of Le Carnaval des animaux (The Carnival of the Animals), for cello and piano. The cello plays a long melody over continuous figuration in the piano.

sections.label: A · Cello melody over piano broken chords
B · Cello melody rises and turns
sections.mNote: Long cello notes over running semiquavers in the piano

sections.label: C · Cello melody in long phrases
sections.mNote: The piano continues its figuration beneath the cello’s sustained melody.

cues.title: Opening, piano and cello
cues.text: The piano sets out G major in broken chords. The cello enters after one bar with a melody that falls twice and then climbs. Each bar has six crotchet beats, and the piano divides them into short, even notes beneath the cello’s longer ones.
cues.evidence: Saint-Saëns, Le Cygne, Durand score, plate D.S. 3891, pp. 1–3; cello part edited by Alvin Buechner, Carl Fischer (1907), opening bars. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/5/5f/IMSLP925269-PMLP06099-2024-03-15-12-42-19-01.PDF
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Dying Swan, 1905
cues.text: In 1905 Anna Pavlova and the choreographer Michel Fokine made this cello solo into The Dying Swan. Saint-Saëns’s movement has twenty-eight bars. The dance became the role most closely associated with Pavlova.
cues.evidence: The ballet’s creation for Pavlova in 1905 is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_cygne, citing Lynn Garafola, Legacies of Twentieth-Century Dance (2005), pp. 155–156. The Durand score has twenty-eight bars.

cues.title: Final bars, held G
cues.text: The last phrase slows and the cello holds a high G, marked pianissimo. The piano continues its broken chords beneath the held note, then finishes alone. The final rest also carries a pause mark.
cues.evidence: Durand score, plate D.S. 3891, p. 3, last five bars; Carl Fischer cello part (1907), last line. The recording is dated around 1925 in its discography: https://archive.org/details/3-judith-bokor-col-d-17144-fx-16-17-kol-nidrei_202309
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Pianist from the age of ten and organist for twenty years, known for the Organ Symphony, a dance of skeletons featuring xylophone, and a zoo suite he forbade anyone to publish.
facts: Piano with Stamaty; organ with François Benoist and composition under Halévy at the Paris Conservatoire, from 1848
Organist of La Madeleine, 1857–77; piano professor at the École Niedermeyer, 1861–65; co-founder of the Société nationale de musique, 1871
Symphonies, ten concertos, four symphonic poems, operas, organ music, songs and chamber music; also plays, poems and articles
Spent most winters from 1873 in Algeria, Egypt or the Canary Islands, and kept no fixed address from 1889 to 1905

quote.text: I have given it all that I had to give. What I have done I shall never do again.
quote.source: Saint-Saëns on the Organ Symphony, as quoted in Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note

composer.background:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born at 3 rue du Jardinet in Paris on 9 October 1835. His father, a clerk in the Ministry of the Interior, died of consumption on 30 December, when the boy was not yet three months old. He was a sickly child and was raised by two widows, his mother Clémence and her aunt Charlotte Masson, who taught him piano. At two and a half he pressed the keys one at a time and waited for each note to die away before playing the next. By his own account he already listened at that age to the kettle on the drawing-room fire, which he called a “microscopic oboe”, and to its sound swelling until the water boiled.

Children’s pieces gave the left hand nothing to do. “The bass doesn’t sing,” he told his teachers in disgust, and was given Haydn and Mozart. On 6 May 1846, aged ten, he played Beethoven’s Third Piano Concerto and a Mozart concerto in B♭ at the Salle Pleyel, and played the whole programme from memory. Someone asked his mother what he would play when he was twenty. “He will play his own,” she said.
